analysis.one_liner: Temporarily enlarges the refundable child tax credit and cuts business taxes on research and equipment investment.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 357–70 with big bipartisan support, but Senate Republicans blocked it from ever reaching a Senate vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two big things at once. It would enlarge the refundable part of the child tax credit for 2023–2025, counting the credit per child so larger families get more, and let some workers use last year's income to qualify for the earned income tax credit. It would also restore and extend business tax breaks: companies could again immediately deduct domestic research costs, fully write off equipment purchases, and deduct more business interest. It would also make wildfire and East Palestine derailment payments tax-free, expand the low-income housing tax credit, cut the tax rate on some Taiwan investors' U.S. income, and raise penalties for promoters of dubious COVID employee-retention credit claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with children get a bigger refundable child tax credit through 2025 — up to $1,900 per child in 2024 and $2,000 in 2025, applied per child so a family with two kids gets twice the refundable amount. Low-income workers with an income dip can use prior-year earnings for the earned income tax credit. Victims of federally declared wildfires and of the East Palestine, Ohio train derailment would not pay tax on compensation payments. Renters benefit from a larger low-income housing tax credit. Businesses get to immediately deduct domestic research spending from 2022 through 2026, full bonus depreciation on equipment, higher expensing limits, and a more generous interest deduction. Some investors and residents of Taiwan pay a 10–15% withholding rate on U.S. income instead of 30%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with kids, businesses, disaster victims

how_it_helps.text: The refundable child tax credit rises to $1,800 per child for 2023, $1,900 for 2024, and $2,000 for 2025, and is calculated per qualifying child, so bigger families get proportionally more back even if they owe little or no income tax.
Workers who earn less in 2024 or 2025 than the prior year can elect to use the prior year's earned income to compute the earned income tax credit, softening the penalty for a bad year.

Compensation for losses from federally declared wildfires (payments received 2020–2025) and payments from the East Palestine train derailment — including from Norfolk Southern and its insurers — are excluded from taxable income.

The low-income housing tax credit ceiling rises from 9% to 12.5% for 2023–2025, and projects can qualify with only 30% bond financing through 2025, supporting more subsidized affordable rental construction.

Companies can expense (immediately deduct) domestic research costs incurred 2022–2026 rather than spreading deductions over years, extend 100% bonus depreciation through 2026, deduct up to $1.29 million of business assets, and use pre-2022 depreciation rules for the interest deduction through 2025.
Some residents of and investors in Taiwan pay reduced withholding — generally 10% on interest, royalties, and gains, 15% (or 10% for corporate holders) on dividends — instead of the default 30%.
The 1099 reporting threshold for contractors rises from $600 to $1,000, cutting paperwork for small payers and low-earning contractors.
Promoters of dubious COVID employee-retention credit claims face much larger penalties, and most pending claims had to be filed by January 31, 2024.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the federal Treasury — that is, current and future taxpayers — because the tax cuts are not paid for with offsetting revenue. The largest share of the cost goes to the business tax provisions, which benefit profitable companies most. The higher contractor reporting threshold slightly reduces the IRS's visibility into contractor income. Renters and affordable-housing tenants benefit only indirectly, through projects that developers choose to build with the expanded credits.

drawbacks.text: Most of the bill's cost goes to business tax breaks — retroactive research expensing, bonus depreciation, and interest deductions — whose benefits flow mainly to profitable companies, not to the families the title emphasizes.

The refundable child tax credit phases in with earnings, so families with little or no earned income — the very poorest — get little or nothing from this expansion; the bill enlarges the credit for families with jobs rather than reaching those without any.
Raising the contractor reporting threshold from $600 to $1,000 reduces tax paperwork but also reduces the information the IRS receives about contractor income.
The child tax credit and business changes are temporary, expiring after 2025, so families and businesses get relief for only a few years unless Congress extends it later at further cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family and disaster provisions deliver real, targeted help: a larger per-child refundable credit for working families, tax-free disaster compensation, and more subsidized housing. But roughly as much of the bill is a set of retroactive and temporary business tax cuts whose benefits concentrate in companies with big capital and research budgets, and none of it is paid for. It is a genuine compromise package that helps ordinary families materially while also handing a substantial tax cut to business.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it easily 357–70, but when the Senate tried on August 1, 2024, a procedural vote (cloture, which needed 60 senators just to begin debating the bill) failed 48–44, so the Senate never got to vote on the bill itself and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was a bipartisan tax deal negotiated by House Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith and reported out of committee 40–3 on January 19, 2024.
On January 31, 2024, the House passed it under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority, voting 357–70, with 188 of 216 Democrats and 169 of 224 Republicans in favor.
The bill sat on the Senate calendar for months; Majority Leader Schumer made a motion to proceed in July 2024 and filed a cloture motion to force the issue.
On August 1, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 48–44, short of the 60 needed: 43 of 48 Democrats but only 3 of 49 Republicans voted yes, with 41 Senate Republicans voting no.
The Senate never voted on the bill itself, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senate Republicans who opposed the bill got what they wanted: it never came to a vote. The Treasury keeps the revenue the tax cuts would have cost, but families lost the larger child tax credit and businesses kept the research-cost deduction rules they had pushed to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Senate opponents; Treasury keeps the revenue

sides.party_line_note: House passage was bipartisan — 188 of 216 Democrats and 169 of 224 Republicans voted yes — but the decisive Senate vote split by party: 43 of 48 Democrats voted to begin debate while only 3 of 49 Republicans did, with 41 Republicans voting no.

industries.note: The bill lets companies immediately deduct domestic research costs and fully write off equipment through 2026, a multi-year tax cut that falls most heavily on profitable capital-intensive firms. Its cost is carried by the Treasury, meaning all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers and tax-credit investors
industries.note: The low-income housing tax credit expansion increases the subsidy that flows to developers and the investors who buy the credits, while producing more subsidized rental housing. The public benefit arrives through — and reinforces — this tax-credit financing channel.

Reduced withholding on U.S.-source income for qualified residents of Taiwan lowers the cost of cross-border investment and eases double taxation. The U.S. Treasury collects less withholding on those payments.
Raising the 1099 reporting threshold to $1,000 cuts paperwork for small payers and low-earning contractors, but also reduces the income information reported to the IRS.

The bill sharply raises penalties for promoters who take a cut of questionable COVID employee-retention credit claims and cuts off most late claims. This targets companies that profited from dubious filings at the expense of the Treasury.
